# Solving for Price: Inverse Demand

{{< include _common.qmd >}}

Demand functions are usually written with quantity as a function of price, such
as $Q = 120 - 4P$ (quantity demanded depends on price, or $Q$ is a function of $P$). However, in economics we typically put price on the vertical axis when graphing. Also, some problems may ask "what price clears the market if $Q$ units are sold?" For both reasons you'll often want to use the **inverse demand curve**: the same relationship solved for $P$ as a function of $Q$.

## The method

Start from $Q = a - bP$ and isolate $P$:

$$
\begin{aligned}
bP &= a - Q \\
P &= \frac{a}{b} - \frac{1}{b}\,Q
\end{aligned}
$$

So the inverse demand curve has intercept $a/b$ and slope $-1/b$.

::: {.callout-note}
## Example
If $Q = 120 - 4P$, then $4P = 120 - Q$, so $P = 30 - 0.25Q$.
The intercept, 30, is the **choke price**: the price at which quantity
demanded falls to zero.
:::

::: {.callout-warning}
## Common mistake
The slope of the inverse demand curve is $-1/b$, **not** $-b$. Solving for
$P$ means dividing *everything* by $b$, including the coefficient on $Q$.
:::
